newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine reformer quits, angry at budget delays.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine reformer quits, angry at budget delays.

text.p: Ukraine's leading economic reformer tendered his resignation on Wednesday, accusing parliament and the government of dragging their heels on approving the 1997 budget and tax changes needed to underpin the spending plans.

The presidential press service said it was not yet clear if President Leonid Kuchma would accept the resignation of deputy prime minister Viktor Pynzenyk. But a spokesman said Pynzenyk had made his anger clear in a letter of resignation. "Pynzenyk said he was disenchanted with the government's programmes and priorities, and was extremely unhappy with how the government was doing things to pass reforms," Kuchma's chief spokesman Yevhen Kushnaryov told reporters.
Western diplomats were dismayed at the probable departure of the 42-year-old economics professor, who had been in charge of Ukraine's reform programme since 1994.

"The problem is that if you get rid of Pynzenyk, who in the government will know what they're doing?" said one diplomat. "He was not charismatic but he had a notion of what economic reforms were about, he had the instincts and the academic background."

Pynzenyk took much of the credit for the successful introduction of the hryvnia currency last year, and his tough policies helped bring inflation down to 39.7 percent in 1995. Inflation is forecast at 25 percent this year.

He kept a cot in his office as he worked around the clock to pull Ukraine out of its economic crisis, but he had sounded increasingly bitter in recent months as he complained about low foreign investment and ineffective reforms.
He became frustrated at parliamentary delays in passing the budget, which could pave the way for Ukraine to receive a $2.5 to $3 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund.
The document was due for parliamentary approval on January 1. But the former Soviet republic has not succeeded in passing a budget on time since independence in 1991.

Ukraine's economy has shrunk stubbornly in the five years since independence, wage debts have risen to $3.1 billion, foreign investment levels have been tiny, corruption is rife, and the potentially profitable agriculture sector is in tatters.
Serhiy Teryokhyn, leader of the Reform group in the conservative-dominated parliament, said Kuchma was likely to accept Pynzenyk's resignation.

"There is no reason for Pynzenyk to remain in government. He's a liberal economic reformer and the prime minister has been pushing opposing views," he said, blaming Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko for rolling back reforms during nine months in office.

Lazarenko, criticised by Kuchma in his state of the nation address last month, had been expected to speak in parliament on Wednesday, addressing the possibility of a cabinet reshuffle and a reduction in the number of ministries.
But the appearance was postponed and no new date has been set for Lazarenko to talk to parliament, which is dominated by communists and other conservatives.
Kuchma on Wednesday sacked the heads of Ukraine's top nuclear and energy bodies, but there was no news on ministerial changes.

The sackings were first announced last week by Volodymyr Horbulin, secretary of Kuchma's policy-making Security and Defence Council, who cited problems such as unpaid bills to Ukraine's five nuclear power plants and nuclear fuel shortages.
